body.statement:
Under \(d^\star\), let \(b_{n,\varepsilon}=\mathbb P_{d^\star}(G_n(\varepsilon)^c)\). On \(G_n(\varepsilon)\),
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}\mid F)
 =\sigma^2(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1},
\]
and
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2}{n(1+\varepsilon)}\Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}
 \preceq\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}\mid F)
 \preceq
 \frac{\sigma^2}{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}.
\]
Unconditionally,
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 =\sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[
 \mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}
 \operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}\right]
 +\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
 b_{n,\varepsilon}\le
 \min\!\left\{1,2q\exp\!\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right)\right\}
 =\min\{1,\delta_{n,\varepsilon}\},
\]
and
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}\frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon}}{1+\varepsilon}
 \le R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}+B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}(1+2\varepsilon)
 +2B^2q\exp\!\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right).
\]
For the fixed threshold \(\bar\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), the second-order inverse identity gives the sharper relative-risk bound
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left|
 \frac{R_n(\beta,\sigma,\bar\varepsilon)}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star/n}-1
 \right|
 &\le
 \frac{\mu^\star-1}{(1-\bar\varepsilon)n}
 +\left(1+\mu^\star+
 \frac{n\|\beta\|_2^2}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}\right)b_{n,\bar\varepsilon}\\
 &\le
 \frac{\mu^\star-1}{(1-\bar\varepsilon)n}
 +2q\left(1+\mu^\star+
 \frac{nB^2}{\sigma_{\min}^2\Phi^\star}\right)
 \exp\!\left(-\frac{n\bar\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
body.justification: The theorem verifies the exact Chernoff constant, preserves fallback bias, and exploits mean-zero whitened-Gram fluctuations to give an explicit second-order relative-risk error.
body.gap: Tropp supplies the matrix tail inequality and general random-design regression work supplies conditioning templates, but neither gives this product-Fourier leverage calibration, fallback branch, or fixed-threshold second-order constant.
body.consumer: The result turns the exact population design into an auditable finite-sample precision guarantee and supplies the quantitative input for fixed-dimensional oracle attainment.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(\Sigma=\Sigma_k(d^\star)\). The supply-range assumption and the uniform-dosage definition give \(0<u\le1/2\), hence \(d^\star\in(0,1)^p\). By \(\textnormal{lem:trace-identity}\), \(\Sigma\) is positive definite, so all inverse square roots below exist and \(0<\Phi^\star=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1})<\infty\).

Define the proof-intermediate whitened row \(w_a=\Sigma^{-1/2}x_a\) and the rank-one matrix \(K_a=w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}\). Product randomization across units and the definition of \(\Sigma\) imply that \(K_1,\ldots,K_n\) are independent, positive semidefinite, and
\[
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}K_a
 =\Sigma^{-1/2}\mathbb E_{d^\star}(x_ax_a^{\mathsf T})\Sigma^{-1/2}
 =I_q. \tag{1}
\]
The exact-leverage proposition gives, at every point of the finite assignment support,
\[
 \lambda_{\max}(K_a)=\|w_a\|_2^2
 =x_a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}x_a\le\mu^\star. \tag{2}
\]
In particular, \(0\preceq K_a\preceq\mu^\star I_q\). The exact formula in \(\textnormal{prop:exact-leverage}\) also shows \(\mu^\star>1\).

Apply \(\textnormal{lem:tropp-matrix-chernoff}\) with summand bound \(R=\mu^\star\). Equation \((1)\) gives
\[
 \sum_{a=1}^n\mathbb E K_a=nI_q,
 \qquad \mu_{\min}=\mu_{\max}=n. \tag{3}
\]
For \(0\le t\le1/2\), define
\[
 h_+(t)=(1+t)\log(1+t)-t,
 \qquad h_-(t)=t+(1-t)\log(1-t).
\]
Both functions and their first derivatives vanish at zero, while
\[
 h_+''(t)=\frac1{1+t}\ge\frac23,
 \qquad h_-''(t)=\frac1{1-t}\ge1.
\]
Twice integrating these inequalities from zero gives \(h_+(t)\ge t^2/3\) and \(h_-(t)\ge t^2/2\ge t^2/3\). Since
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{a=1}^nK_a
 =\Sigma^{-1/2}(F^{\mathsf T}F/n)\Sigma^{-1/2}
 =I_q+H_n(\varepsilon), \tag{4}
\]
the two matrix-Chernoff tails, followed by the union bound, yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P_{d^\star}\!\left\{\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{a=1}^nK_a\right)\le1-\varepsilon\right\}
 &\le q\exp\!\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right),\\
 \mathbb P_{d^\star}\!\left\{\lambda_{\max}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{a=1}^nK_a\right)\ge1+\varepsilon\right\}
 &\le q\exp\!\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
and therefore
\[
 b_{n,\varepsilon}
 \le\min\!\left\{1,2q\exp\!\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right)\right\}
 =\min\{1,\delta_{n,\varepsilon}\}. \tag{5}
\]
This verifies the displayed Chernoff constant from the primitive independence, isotropy, and leverage bound rather than assuming a Gram limit law.

On \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), equations \((4)\) and the definition of the operator norm imply
\[
 (1-\varepsilon)\Sigma
 \preceq F^{\mathsf T}F/n
 \preceq(1+\varepsilon)\Sigma. \tag{6}
\]
Because \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) and \(\Sigma\succ0\), the empirical Gram matrix is invertible on this event. Inversion reverses Loewner order, so
\[
 \frac1{n(1+\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}
 \preceq(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}
 \preceq\frac1{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}. \tag{7}
\]
The linear-response assumption and the estimator definition give, conditionally on any \(F\in G_n(\varepsilon)\),
\[
 \widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}-\beta
 =(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}F^{\mathsf T}\epsilon.
\]
Conditional centering makes this error conditionally mean zero. Conditional homoskedasticity then gives the exact covariance
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}\mid F)
 &=(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}F^{\mathsf T}(\sigma^2I_n)F(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\\
 &=\sigma^2(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}. \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
The variance-range assumption supplies \(\sigma\ge\sigma_{\min}>0\). Multiplying \((7)\) by \(\sigma^2\) proves the conditional covariance sandwich.

The causal coefficient vector is not being defined by an observed-law functional. Indeed, linear response, iterated expectation, and conditional centering prove
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]
 &=\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_ax_a^{\mathsf T}]\beta
   +\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_a\epsilon_a]\\
 &=\Sigma\beta+
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[x_a\mathbb E(\epsilon_a\mid F)\right]
 =\Sigma\beta.
\end{aligned}
\]
The already-established invertibility of \(\Sigma\) consequently identifies the causal target as \(\beta=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]\).

The event \(G_n(\varepsilon)\) is measurable with respect to \(F\). On it, equation \((8)\) and conditional centering show
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left(\|\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}-\beta\|_2^2\mid F\right)
 =\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}.
\]
On its complement the estimator is zero, so its squared error equals \(\|\beta\|_2^2\). Splitting over these two events gives the exact unconditional decomposition
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 =\sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[
 \mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}\operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}\right]
 +\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}. \tag{9}
\]
Thus no bias contribution from the fallback branch has been discarded. Taking traces in \((7)\), using \(\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1})=\Phi^\star\), and then using \(\|\beta\|_2\le B\), proves
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}\frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon}}{1+\varepsilon}
 \le R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}+B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}. \tag{10}
\]
Since \((1-\varepsilon)^{-1}\le1+2\varepsilon\) for \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), substitution of \((5)\) into \((10)\) proves the remaining first-order upper bound.

It remains to establish the fixed-threshold second-order conclusion. Fix \(\bar\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) as in \(\textnormal{def:oracle-threshold}\), abbreviate \(\overline G=G_n(\bar\varepsilon)\), \(b=b_{n,\bar\varepsilon}\), \(H=H_n(\bar\varepsilon)\), and put \(D=\Sigma^{-1}\). Equations \((1)\) and \((4)\) imply
\[
 H=\frac1n\sum_{a=1}^n(K_a-I_q),
 \qquad \mathbb EH=0. \tag{11}
\]
Because \(K_a\) is rank one, \(K_a^2=\|w_a\|_2^2K_a\). Equation \((2)\) therefore gives
\[
 K_a^2\preceq\mu^\star K_a,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E(K_a-I_q)^2=\mathbb EK_a^2-I_q
 \preceq(\mu^\star-1)I_q. \tag{12}
\]
For \(a\ne c\), independence and centering give \(\mathbb E[(K_a-I_q)(K_c-I_q)]=0\). Expanding the square in \((11)\) and applying \((12)\) yields
\[
 \mathbb EH^2
 =\frac1{n^2}\sum_{a=1}^n\mathbb E(K_a-I_q)^2
 \preceq\frac{\mu^\star-1}{n}I_q. \tag{13}
\]

On \(\overline G\), the spectrum of \(I_q+H\) lies in \([1-\bar\varepsilon,1+\bar\varepsilon]\). The exact algebraic identity
\[
 (I_q+H)^{-1}=I_q-H+H^2(I_q+H)^{-1} \tag{14}
\]
follows by multiplying both sides by \(I_q+H\). Moreover, \(H\) commutes with \((I_q+H)^{-1}\), so \(H^2(I_q+H)^{-1}\) is positive semidefinite and
\[
 0\preceq H^2(I_q+H)^{-1}
 \preceq\frac1{1-\bar\varepsilon}H^2
 \quad\hbox{on }\overline G. \tag{15}
\]
Since \(D\succeq0\), equations \((13)\)--\((15)\) give
\[
 0\le
 \mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf 1_{\overline G}
 \operatorname{tr}\{DH^2(I_q+H)^{-1}\}\right]
 \le\frac{\mu^\star-1}{(1-\bar\varepsilon)n}\operatorname{tr}(D). \tag{16}
\]

The global bounds \(0\preceq n^{-1}\sum_aK_a\preceq\mu^\star I_q\), which follow from \((2)\), imply \(-I_q\preceq H\preceq(\mu^\star-1)I_q\), hence \(\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\mu^\star\). Therefore
\[
 |\operatorname{tr}(DH)|
 \le\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\operatorname{tr}(D)
 \le\mu^\star\Phi^\star. \tag{17}
\]
Taking the \(D\)-weighted trace in \((14)\), restricting to \(\overline G\), and using \(\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}(DH)=0\) from \((11)\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf 1_{\overline G}
 \operatorname{tr}\{D(I_q+H)^{-1}\}\right]-\Phi^\star\\
 &\quad=-b\Phi^\star
 +\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf 1_{\overline G^c}\operatorname{tr}(DH)\right]
 +\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf 1_{\overline G}
 \operatorname{tr}\{DH^2(I_q+H)^{-1}\}\right]. \tag{18}
\end{aligned}
\]
Equations \((16)\)--\((18)\) and the triangle inequality prove
\[
 \left|
 \frac{\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\overline G}
 \operatorname{tr}\{D(I_q+H)^{-1}\}]}{\Phi^\star}-1
 \right|
 \le\frac{\mu^\star-1}{(1-\bar\varepsilon)n}
 +(1+\mu^\star)b. \tag{19}
\]
Finally, on \(\overline G\), congruence in \((4)\) gives
\[
 \operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}
 =\frac1n\operatorname{tr}\{D(I_q+H)^{-1}\}.
\]
Substitute this identity into the exact decomposition \((9)\), divide by the positive quantity \(\sigma^2\Phi^\star/n\), and apply \((19)\). This yields
\[
 \left|
 \frac{R_n(\beta,\sigma,\bar\varepsilon)}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star/n}-1
 \right|
 \le\frac{\mu^\star-1}{(1-\bar\varepsilon)n}
 +\left(1+\mu^\star+
 \frac{n\|\beta\|_2^2}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}\right)b.
\]
Using \(\|\beta\|_2\le B\), \(\sigma\ge\sigma_{\min}>0\), and the fixed-threshold instance of \((5)\) proves the final displayed inequality. The proof used exactly the stipulated conditional first and second noise moments; it neither assumes conditional Gaussianity nor compares finite-sample risk across dosage designs.
